title: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table
description: Brute force to optimized: generating and sorting all m*n entries versus binary search on the value, using an O(m) row-counting formula.

sections.title: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table

content.title: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the height m and width n of an m by n multiplication table (where the entry at row i, column j is i times j, both 1-indexed), and an integer k, return the k-th smallest number in this table.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","m (rows), n (columns), k"],["Output","The k-th smallest value among all m*n table entries"],["Goal","Find the answer without generating all m*n entries, exploiting a countable, monotonic structure"],["Constraints","1 <= m, n <= 3*10^4, 1 <= k <= m*n"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"k-th smallest value in an implicitly huge structured collection\"","Binary search on the answer value, counting how many entries are <= a candidate"],["Each row of the multiplication table is itself sorted (row i is i, 2i, 3i, ..., ni)","Counting entries <= x in a single row has a direct O(1) formula: min(n, floor(x/i))"]]}

blocks.text: Row i of the table consists of i, 2i, 3i, ..., ni, in increasing order. For any candidate value x, the number of entries in row i that are <= x is exactly min(n, floor(x/i)), a direct formula requiring no scanning. Summing this across all m rows gives the total count of table entries <= x in O(m) time, letting binary search find the k-th smallest value directly.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Times Tables Entries Fall Below a Threshold
blocks.text: Picture a classroom times-table poster, and asking how many entries on the whole poster are less than or equal to some number x. For any single row (the multiples of a particular number), counting how many of its entries are <= x is immediate, since they are evenly spaced multiples; adding this up across every row directly gives the total count.

blocks.caption: Each row's count of entries <= x has a direct formula; summing over all rows counts the whole table

blocks.text: Result: 3. The 3x3 table is [1,2,3 / 2,4,6 / 3,6,9]; sorted, it reads [1,2,2,3,3,4,6,6,9], and the 5th smallest is 3.

Before generating and sorting all m*n entries, notice that counting how many table entries are <= a candidate value x has a direct O(m) formula (summing min(n, floor(x/i)) across rows), and this count is monotonically non-decreasing in x, making binary search on x directly applicable.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Row i contains the values i, 2i, ..., ni; the count of these that are <= x is exactly floor(x/i), capped at n (since the row only has n entries).

Observation 2: Summing min(n, floor(x/i)) over all rows i from 1 to m gives the total count of table entries <= x, computable directly in O(m) without generating any entries.

Observation 3: This count is monotonically non-decreasing as x increases, exactly the structure binary search on the answer exploits.

Observation 4: Binary searching over x in [1, m*n], finding the smallest x for which the count of entries <= x is at least k, gives the k-th smallest value directly (this smallest such x IS guaranteed to be an actual table entry, since counts only change at table-entry values).
This leads to binary searching over candidate values x in [1, m*n], counting table entries <= x via the row formula in O(m), and finding the smallest x where this count reaches at least k.
Generate every entry i*j for 1<=i<=m, 1<=j<=n, sort all m*n values, and return the k-th smallest.

items: Generate every product i*j for i in [1,m], j in [1,n].
Return the value at index k-1 in this sorted list.

codes.python:
def find_kth_number_brute(m, n, k):
    values = [i * j for i in range(1, m + 1) for j in range(1, n + 1)]  # generate ALL entries
    values.sort()
    return values[k - 1]

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Generating and sorting all entries directly gives the exact k-th smallest, guaranteed correct.
This costs O(m*n log(m*n)) time and O(m*n) space, infeasible for m, n up to 3*10^4 (up to 9*10^8 entries).

blocks.text: Limitation: generating and storing all m*n entries is infeasible at scale; binary search combined with the O(m) row-counting formula achieves O(m log(m*n)) without ever generating a single entry.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating all entries is unnecessary: only the COUNT of entries <= a candidate value is needed at each binary search step, not the entries themselves.

The row-counting formula: since row i is i, 2i, ..., ni, the count of entries in that row which are <= x is min(n, floor(x/i)), computable in O(1) per row, O(m) total per candidate x.

Applying binary search: search x in [1, m*n]; if the total count of entries <= x is at least k, x might still be reducible (search smaller); otherwise, x needs to be larger.

The core idea: binary search on the candidate value, using the O(m) row-counting formula as the monotonic feasibility check, entirely avoiding generating the table.

Binary search x in [1, m*n]. At each step, compute the count of table entries <= x using the row formula (summed over all m rows in O(m)); if this count is >= k, move hi to x (search smaller); otherwise move lo to x+1.
Dry run for m=3, n=3, k=5

blocks.caption: Binary search on the value, using the O(m) row-counting formula as the feasibility check

blocks.text: Since each row is a simple arithmetic sequence, the count of its entries at or below any threshold x has an exact closed-form formula, avoiding any need to enumerate row entries directly. Summing this formula across all m rows correctly counts the ENTIRE table's entries <= x in O(m). Because this total count is monotonically non-decreasing in x, binary search correctly converges on the smallest x for which the count reaches at least k, and since counts only change at actual table-entry values, this smallest x is guaranteed to itself be a genuine table entry, exactly the k-th smallest.

blocks.text: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table is a strong example of "binary search on the answer with an implicit counting formula," avoiding generating a structure that could be astronomically large.

items: Forgetting to cap each row's count at n (a row only has n entries, even if floor(x/i) would suggest more).
Using floating-point division instead of integer division for floor(x/i), risking precision errors.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k = 1","Returns 1, the smallest entry in any multiplication table."],["k = m*n","Returns m*n, the largest entry (at the bottom-right corner)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly deriving the row-counting formula (min(n, floor(x/i))) and explaining why it enables O(m) counting without generating any entries is the key insight to state clearly before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "k-th smallest value in an implicitly huge, structured collection", think: binary search on the value, using a direct O(1)-per-row (or per-group) counting formula.

items: How would you adapt this if the table used addition (i+j) instead of multiplication?
How would you find the k-th smallest sum of two sorted arrays using a similar counting technique?

Any "k-th smallest value in an implicit combinatorial structure" problem, solvable via binary search with a closed-form or efficiently computable count.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Generating and sorting all entries costs O(m*n log(m*n)) time and O(m*n) space; binary search with the row-counting formula costs O(m log(m*n)) time and O(1) space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer value, using a direct O(1)-per-row counting formula.
Core Idea: binary search x in [1, m*n]; count entries <= x via sum of min(n, floor(x/i)) over all rows; converge on the smallest x with count >= k.
Time: O(m*n log(m*n)) for generating and sorting, O(m log(m*n)) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: each row's count of entries below a threshold has a direct formula, avoiding the need to ever generate the table.
Interview Difficulty: a clever binary-search-with-counting problem, non-obvious until the row formula is recognized.
One line memory trick: binary search the value; count entries per row via min(n, x/i), summed across rows.
